name: Letrozole

lead: Letrozole is a prescription aromatase inhibitor for postmenopausal breast cancer and is also widely used in fertility treatment. Looksmax.org users, including teenagers, discuss it for delaying growth-plate closure to add height, and some link lower oestrogen to leanness.

It blocks the aromatase enzyme, lowering conversion of androgens to oestrogen. Since oestrogen drives growth-plate fusion, the hope is a longer growth window. No controlled trial in healthy adolescents testing it for adult height was found, and forum users describe it as the most potent option and the most likely to crash oestrogen.

paras: Heightmaxxers discuss it alongside growth hormone or MK-677 and compare it with anastrozole and exemestane. It is prescription-only, and height use is off-label.

The label lists bone density loss, raised cholesterol, fatigue and dizziness, hot flashes and joint pain, and it can cause fetal harm and is contraindicated in pregnancy. Height use is off-label and untested in adolescents.

angle.text: Letrozole lowers oestrogen strongly, and heightmaxxers hope this delays growth-plate closure for extra adult height; some users also link low oestrogen to leanness. Trials cover breast cancer and fertility, not height in healthy people.

lead: Letrozole is an oral, non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor: it blocks the enzyme that converts androgens into oestrogens. The US label lists adjuvant and extended adjuvant treatment of hormone receptor-positive early breast cancer in postmenopausal women and first- and second-line treatment of advanced disease, and it is also a standard ovulation-induction drug in fertility medicine.[1][2][3] Its appearance-related interest is height: oestrogen drives growth-plate maturation in both sexes, so people who want extra centimetres reason that lowering oestrogen during adolescence could slow skeletal maturation and lengthen the growth window.[4][5]

On looksmax.org it is discussed under heightmaxxing, often alongside growth hormone or MK-677, with users comparing it with anastrozole and exemestane (Aromasin) and many describing it as the most potent of the three.[6][7][8][9] Paediatric endocrinologists have studied aromatase inhibitors, including letrozole, in boys with idiopathic short stature or delayed puberty since the early 2000s. Short-term results show slower bone-age advance and higher predicted adult height, while measured final height data are sparse and mixed.[5][10][11][12]
The label warns of decreased bone mineral density, raised cholesterol, fatigue and dizziness, and embryo-fetal toxicity, and letrozole is a prescription-only medicine.[1][3]
infobox: Breast cancer in postmenopausal women (US label) [1]
Height (adolescent growth-plate timing); oestrogen control during testosterone use
Prescription-only in the US, UK and EU; Schedule VII in Canada [3]

paras: Letrozole is a selective, reversible aromatase inhibitor that binds the heme group of the aromatase cytochrome P450 enzyme, cutting oestrogen production without reducing corticosteroids. Wikipedia describes high oral bioavailability, an elimination half-life of about two days, and metabolism to inactive compounds excreted mainly by the kidneys.[3][13] It belongs to the third generation of aromatase inhibitors, alongside anastrozole and exemestane; exemestane is steroidal and irreversible, whereas letrozole and anastrozole are non-steroidal and reversible.[4]

Because aromatase is the main route to oestrogen in postmenopausal women, the drug has been used chiefly in that group. In men and adolescents, blocking aromatase lowers oestradiol while testosterone typically rises, an effect that underlies both the paediatric growth research and the use of aromatase inhibitors by some testosterone users.[3][12]

The US label covers early and advanced hormone receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women.[1] Randomised trials compared letrozole with tamoxifen in early disease (the BIG 1-98 comparison, reported in 2005), tested it after five years of tamoxifen, and combined it with CDK4/6 inhibitors such as palbociclib and ribociclib.[14][15][16][17][18] Wikipedia notes that BIG 1-98 reduced recurrence compared with tamoxifen without changing survival.[3]

In reproductive medicine, letrozole is recommended as a first-line ovulation inducer in polycystic ovary syndrome and was first studied against clomiphene around 2001; a Cochrane review and a meta-analysis in unexplained infertility examine its use.[19][3] Other investigated uses listed by Wikipedia include gynecomastia, male infertility, endometriosis, uterine fibroids and growth delay in adolescents.[3]

Height is the main appearance goal. Users who believe their growth plates are still open (typically teenagers and young adults) discuss whether suppressing oestrogen could keep the plates open longer so that growth hormone, MK-677 or natural growth can continue.[6][8][20] Threads ask which inhibitor is best for height, how letrozole compares with Aromasin, and where to obtain it.[7][21][9]

A second, smaller thread of discussion concerns body composition and oestrogen control during testosterone use. On T Nation a user planning a testosterone cycle discusses aromatase-inhibitor choice and measurement difficulties with powders.[22] Wikipedia notes that the World Anti-Doping Agency lists aromatase inhibitors as prohibited because they can counter side effects of anabolic steroids, while stating letrozole itself is not a performance enhancer.[3]

No trial has tested letrozole for height in healthy adolescents of normal stature. Paediatric trials have enrolled boys with idiopathic short stature, constitutional delay of puberty or growth hormone deficiency, and their results differ by age, drug and combination.[10][23]

A double-blind placebo-controlled trial of 31 boys with idiopathic short stature aged 9 to 14.5, reported in 2005, gave letrozole or placebo for two years. Predicted adult height rose by 5.9 cm in the letrozole group and was unchanged with placebo, bone maturation slowed, and bone mineral density changes were similar between groups.[5]

A 2015 Cochrane review of four randomised trials (207 participants) of aromatase inhibitors in short boys found improved short-term growth measures including predicted adult height, but only one trial reported near-final height, from a non-randomised extension. It also reported mild vertebral abnormalities in 45 percent of prepubertal boys with idiopathic short stature on letrozole versus none on placebo.[10]

A 2016 three-arm trial of 76 pubertal boys with severe idiopathic short stature compared an aromatase inhibitor, growth hormone, and both for 24 to 36 months. Near-final height gains were about 18.2 cm, 20.6 cm and 22.5 cm respectively, with similar safety outcomes across groups.[24] A 2019 long-term follow-up of a placebo-controlled trial in 20 pre- and early-pubertal boys found adult height of 164.8 cm with letrozole and 163.7 cm with placebo (not significantly different) and no excess of vertebral deformity at follow-up.[11]

A 2024 three-year randomised trial in pubertal boys compared anastrozole with letrozole. Letrozole produced higher testosterone, lower oestradiol and IGF-1, and slower bone-age advance, but predicted adult height changes did not differ between drugs; both groups gained about 1.3 cm in predicted height.[12] A 2021 review concluded that firm conclusions are limited by missing attained-height data and that aromatase inhibitor safety data conflict.[23]

Outside growth research, human trials are overwhelmingly in breast cancer and infertility, including MONALEESA and PALOMA combination trials and a registered 2018 trial of letrozole in stimulated IVF cycles.[16][17][18][25]

The US label lists decreases in bone mineral density, increases in cholesterol, and fatigue, dizziness and somnolence as warnings. Reactions occurring in more than 20 percent of patients include hot flashes, arthralgia, flushing, asthenia, oedema, headache, dizziness, hypercholesterolaemia, increased sweating, bone pain and musculoskeletal symptoms.[1] The label states letrozole can cause fetal harm, is contraindicated in pregnancy, and carries postmarketing reports of spontaneous abortions and congenital defects.[1]

Wikipedia describes the effects as resembling low oestrogen and notes that long-term use raises osteoporosis concern; the aromatase-inhibitor article adds that decreased bone maturation and growth are a recognised paediatric effect, and that men may not show the same bone effects seen in women.[3][4] In the short-stature trials, vertebral deformities were a specific monitored outcome.[10][11] Forum users also raise the risk: one reply says exemestane is safer and harder to crash oestrogen with, while letrozole is the likelier to over-suppress it.[7]

Letrozole inhibits aromatase, the enzyme that converts androstenedione and testosterone to oestrone and oestradiol, lowering circulating oestrogen.[1][13] In adolescents, oestrogen acts on the growth plate in both sexes to promote maturation and eventual fusion; the rationale in paediatric research is that reduced oestrogen decelerates growth-plate fusion and gives growth more time.[4][5]

Wikipedia reports about 99.9 percent oral bioavailability, around 60 percent protein binding and a half-life of roughly two days. It inhibits CYP2A6 and, less strongly, CYP2C19 in vitro, though no clinically relevant interactions with cimetidine or warfarin have been observed.[3]

Aromatase inhibitors descend from first-generation drugs such as aminoglutethimide and testolactone, through second-generation fadrozole and formestane, to the third generation. Wikipedia credits pharmacologist Angela Brodie with pioneering the field, with formestane trials in 1982.[4] Letrozole was patented in 1986 and approved for medical use in 1996; Novartis developed it as Femara.[3]

Its use in fertility began around 2001 when aromatase inhibitors were studied for ovulation induction.[19] Research into aromatase inhibitors for growth in boys followed in the 2000s, including the 2005 randomised trial in idiopathic short stature.[5] The aromatase-inhibitor article cites a 2006 report that letrozole in adolescence increased near-final height in boys with constitutional delay of puberty.[4]

Letrozole is prescription-only in the UK, US and EU and is listed under Schedule VII of Canada's Controlled Drugs and Substances Act.[3] India banned its use for infertility in 2011, citing infant risks, and a 2012 parliamentary committee alleged regulatory collusion with manufacturers.[3] Height use in healthy adolescents is off-label.

Many threads are started by teenagers asking how to obtain letrozole, usually with growth hormone or MK-677, and some mention doing so without parental knowledge.[6][8][21] Responses range from encouragement to suggestions of alternatives such as endoxifen and warnings about risking health for small height gains.[20] One thread title credits letrozole with a dramatic change in attitudes toward women, reflecting anecdotal accounts of mood and hormone effects.[26]

The forum discussion mirrors a debate in paediatric endocrinology about whether skeletal maturation should be manipulated for height. The 2021 review lays out the case for and against, and the 2019 and 2024 trials show that effects depend on age, drug and combination.[11][12][23]
